questions.question: What is a branch in Git?
options: A movable label that points to one commit and moves forward when you commit
A full copy of the project's files in a separate folder
A list of all commits made by one developer
A separate repository that shares a remote
questions.explanation: A branch is just a name for a commit, stored as a tiny file containing a hash. Creating one is instant and costs almost nothing, which is why Git encourages a branch per feature or fix.

questions.question: Which command creates a new branch `feature/login` and switches to it?
questions.explanation: `-c` means create. The classic equivalent is `git checkout -b feature/login`. `git branch feature/login` only creates the branch; you stay on the current one.

questions.question: You're on `feature/login` and want to go back to `main`. Which command?
questions.explanation: `git switch main` (or `git checkout main`) updates your files to match `main` and makes it the current branch. `git switch -` jumps back to the previous branch, like `cd -`.

questions.question: What does `HEAD` refer to?
options: The commit you currently have checked out, usually through the current branch
The newest commit in the repository
The latest commit on the remote
questions.explanation: `HEAD` normally points to a branch name (such as `main`), which points to a commit. When you commit, the branch that `HEAD` points to moves forward. `cat .git/HEAD` shows something like `ref: refs/heads/main`.

questions.question: Which command lists your local branches **and** the remote-tracking branches such as `origin/main`?
questions.explanation: `git branch` lists local branches (the current one marked with `*`), `-r` lists only remote-tracking ones, and `-a` lists both. Run `git fetch` first to make sure the remote ones are up to date.

questions.question: Which command shows, for every local branch, which remote branch it tracks and how many commits it is ahead or behind?
questions.explanation: `-vv` shows each branch's last commit plus its upstream in brackets, such as `[origin/main: ahead 2, behind 1]`. The ahead/behind numbers are based on your last `git fetch`.

questions.question: `feature/login` has been merged into `main` and you're done with it. Which command deletes the local branch?
questions.explanation: `-d` deletes the branch only if it is merged, as a safety check. `-D` deletes it regardless, so unmerged commits are only reachable through the reflog afterwards. You can't delete the branch you're on, so switch away first.

questions.question: How do you delete the branch `feature/login` on GitHub (the remote `origin`) from the command line?
questions.explanation: Deleting on the server is a push. The short form is `git push origin :feature/login` (push "nothing" to that name). `git branch -d -r origin/feature/login` only deletes your local remote-tracking copy.

questions.question: You're on a branch called `fix-loign` and notice the typo. How do you rename the current branch?
questions.explanation: `git branch -m <new>` renames the current branch; `git branch -m <old> <new>` renames another one. If the old name was already pushed, push the new name and delete the old one on the remote.

questions.question: You want to clean up: which local branches are already fully merged into `main`?
questions.explanation: `--merged main` lists branches whose tip is reachable from `main`; those are safe to delete with `-d`. `--no-merged` shows the opposite. Branches merged with **squash** on GitHub won't appear here, because their original commits never reached `main`.

questions.question: You want a new branch `hotfix` that starts at older commit `a1b2c3d`, not at your current commit. Which command?
questions.explanation: Both `git branch <name> <start>` and `git switch -c <name> <start>` take a start point: a hash, tag or another branch. A common one is a release tag: `git switch -c hotfix v1.4.0`.

questions.question: You ran `git switch --detach a1b2c3d` to look at old code and made a commit there. Git warns about "detached HEAD". How do you keep that commit?
options: Create a branch while you're on it: `git switch -c experiment`
Nothing: commits in detached HEAD are automatically added to `main`
questions.explanation: In detached HEAD, `HEAD` points straight at a commit instead of a branch. New commits there belong to no branch, so once you switch away nothing points to them and Git eventually deletes them. A branch gives them a name. Lost it already? `git reflog` still has the hash.

questions.question: You have uncommitted changes in `app.js`, and `git switch main` refuses because `main` has a different version of `app.js`. What are your options?
options: Commit the changes, or `git stash` them, then switch
questions.explanation: Git won't overwrite uncommitted work. Changes to files that are the same on both branches are carried along. For conflicting ones, commit them (perhaps as a WIP commit to amend later) or stash them. `git switch -f` would throw them away.

questions.question: A bug fix was committed as `a1b2c3d`. Which command lists the branches that already contain that fix?
questions.explanation: `--contains` lists branches whose history includes that commit; `-a` adds remote branches. `git tag --contains a1b2c3d` answers the same question for releases. A cherry-picked copy has a different hash, so it won't count.
